# botmux 文档

> 飞书话题群 ↔ AI 编程 CLI 桥接

## Other

- [About & Resources](/botmux/en/about.md): botmux — a bridge between Lark topic groups ↔ AI coding CLIs. Open source under the MIT license.
- [Multi-CLI Adapters](/botmux/en/adapters.md): botmux bridges different CLIs / agents through adapters, selected via cliId in bots.json — one-click switching. Local adapters each run as their own process (under the default tmux backend you can tmux attach into the real process; explicit pty/zellij/herdr backends differ); a few are integrated over API / remotely (e.g. Mira, riff) and are not local processes. Applies to: when you want to switch the underlying CLI, or wire up a new tool, and need its cliId and whether it takes a model param. Doesn't apply: strict Codex-compatible distributions and wrappers / gateways (ccr, aiden x claude, …) do not need new adapters — see Codex-compatible distributions and Wrapper / gateway integration below.
- [Session Adopt](/botmux/en/adopt.md): Seamlessly adopt a CLI process that's already running in tmux, Zellij, Herdr, or Orca into botmux, so you can view progress and interact via Lark on your phone. If a CLI is halfway through a task when you have to leave, send /adopt from Lark and keep watching and sending. <video src="https://magic-builder.tos-cn-beijing.volces.com/uploads/1780421531476_adopt-video.aud.mp4" controls preload="metadata" style={{width:'100%',borderRadius:'8px'}}></video> The selection card lists only sessions for the CLI this bot is bound to (a Pi bot won't list Codex/TRAE panes), and excludes botmux's own bmx-* persistent sessions. For tmux, Zellij, and Herdr, picker headings show the workspace while “Target” shows the session/pane locator. Orca headings show the terminal or CLI session title directly, avoiding a duplicate of the working path below. Lists and restore logs retain the title snapshot from adoption; later renames never affect handle identity checks. Orca's internal handle remains the confirm/restore key but is not shown to users. Orca (experimental): Current coverage includes Orca server and same-host SSH relay. Cross-host relays still require the desktop client to remain online. Compatibility can vary with Orca/relay versions, terminal redraw behavior, and each CLI's transcript format; after an upgrade, re-adopt the session and report version details if discovery, rendering, or structured replies regress. Orca supports server mode (a persistent orcad on Linux, with its CLI at ~/.orca/cli/bin/orca) and SSH-relay mode. When Botmux and the SSH terminal run on the same Linux host, Botmux connects directly to the local relay that owns the original PTY and prefers this route over the desktop CLI. You can close your Mac and then send /adopt to continue the original session; discovery, validation, and input work without the desktop client. Cross-host SSH relays still use the desktop CLI and require the desktop to stay connected. Adoption checks the terminal handle, PTY incarnation, workspace, and local process ownership. Older relays without incarnation metadata cannot use direct control. Sessions previously adopted through the desktop relay need to be adopted again once to select the direct local route. Web Terminal retains text screen snapshots: viewing and input work, while source colors, exact cursor state, and mouse modes are not preserved. After desktop disconnection, local relays reconstruct the screen from retained output; a replay beginning partway through a redraw can leave the screen incomplete. Structured replies use the exact CLI process and transcript binding. Trae, Claude Code, and Codex also reconstruct scrollable user/assistant history from that transcript. MTR, Hermes, and other unverified CLIs currently provide basic terminal access only: the live TUI, Lark input, and Web Terminal remain available, but structured transcript replies and scrollable history are not guaranteed. This is a transcript-ownership limitation, not a terminal I/O limitation. MTR's cwd fallback can be ambiguous when several sessions share one directory, while an externally started Hermes session has no Botmux session marker. Botmux does not guess from the newest session in the same directory because that could expose another terminal's conversation.
- [Core-only (apiOnly) API Control](/botmux/en/api-core-only.md): Embed botmux as a controlled HTTP service inside your own system: one process, a fixed port, bound to 127.0.0.1, with no Feishu credentials / bots.json / supervisor / dashboard. Your orchestrator (task runner, CI, backend, sandbox) drives it over HTTP to run a CLI (codex / claude-code / …), poll results, and get a writable web terminal on demand. This doc is for integrators embedding botmux into their own product (e.g. an in-sandbox botmux running codex). If you just want an external system to trigger a normal bot already running in a Feishu group, see Triggering Tasks via API — that covers the trigger/poll/cancel four-state contract. The two are complementary: the same trigger/poll contract applies under core-only; this doc only covers the core-only-specific startup, auth, route boundary, writable terminal, and security model.
- [Programmatic Task Trigger API](/botmux/en/api-task-trigger.md): Let an external system (task orchestrator, CI, backend service…) hand an instruction to a botmux bot over HTTP. The bot runs its CLI as usual; the caller gets a purely programmatic "request → result". The task can stay entirely out of Feishu, or land in a real group / thread — those two things are independent. This page is for client developers: the full contract of POST /api/trigger — request fields, delivery targets, execution modes, idempotency, four-state polling, status/error codes, limits and traps.
- [Architecture overview](/botmux/en/architecture.md): botmux is a thin orchestration layer that translates "Lark events" into "input/output for CLI processes". Core processes and modules:
- [Best Practices](/botmux/en/best-practices.md): Recommended configurations organized by use case. For basic usage, see the individual feature pages; for troubleshooting, see Common pitfalls and the FAQ.
- [bots.json Configuration](/botmux/en/bots-json.md): Configure bots via ~/.botmux/bots.json. Run botmux setup to create it interactively, or edit it by hand. The file is an array; each element is a bot (in production, one bot maps to one dedicated daemon process). Most fields are optional — just larkAppId / larkAppSecret is enough to run; add the rest as needed. Applies to: manually tuning CLI / model / working dir / permissions / sandbox, etc.; for everyday config the dashboard's Bot Config page is preferred (it edits the same bots.json). Run botmux restart to apply changes. There are many fields, listed below grouped by purpose. The vast majority are optional — just larkAppId / larkAppSecret is enough to get running, and you add the rest as needed.
- [Streaming Cards](/botmux/en/cards.md): Every conversation turn produces a live-updating Lark card, your primary window for perceiving and controlling the CLI on your phone or in Lark. Live screenshots of the terminal refreshed onto the card: xterm renders headlessly into an image that faithfully reproduces the CLI's TUI (borders and colors are all there), instead of converting output to Markdown. One click to "Show / Hide output," "Export text," and "Half-page up / down."Live status indicator: the card's header color is the status (a Lark card template, not an emoji dot in the body) — Starting… (yellow) → Working (blue) → Waiting for input (green); when the quota is used up it shows Limit reached (red), turning to Retryable (green) when it can retry. When the main turn has ended but background work it started (a background agent, a run_in_background Bash, a Monitor; Grok background tasks) is still running, the header reads ⏳ Main turn ended · background tasks running (N) (light blue), with N matching the background tasks shown in the web terminal; it returns to Working when a finished task wakes the main agent, and only shows the turn as done once everything has finished.Operate directly from the card: open the Web terminal, 🔑 grab an operation link, close the session, and — when the quota is retryable — "🔁 Resend last task."A fresh card per turn: the previous card freezes as an archive, keeping conversation history clear and traceable; after a session is moved to another group with /relay, the original card also automatically freezes as an archive (buttons removed).A "recoverable" card on close: it carries a "▶️ Resume session" button to click back in anytime; if the CLI supports native resume (the adapter implements buildResumeCommand and a native session id exists), it also includes the native command (e.g. claude --resume <id>) for manual recovery; when unsupported, only botmux's resume button plus a short note is shown.
- [CLI Commands](/botmux/en/cli-commands.md): Manage the daemon and sessions from the terminal. When the daemon is online, botmux delete first asks the owning daemon to run the same lifecycle teardown as /close: evict the in-memory active session, persist the closed state, and clean up the worker, backend, and subscriptions. The local fallback is used only when the owning daemon is confirmed offline. If an online daemon rejects the request or IPC fails, the command fails without a local hard kill. When BOTMUX_COORDINATION_MODE=primary, the durable PostgreSQL Session is the canonical truth. In this mode, delete, resume, non-dry-run suspend, maintenance suspend-idle, and delete/wake actions in the interactive list are rejected explicitly. list remains available as a read-only local view, but skips local auto-pruning. Use the session card in the original topic to close or resume through the fenced durable session-control lane.
- [Local Companion API](/botmux/en/companion-api.md): Botmux can expose a closed local management protocol for one explicitly bound isolated test Bot. It neither reuses Dashboard tokens or Dashboard/daemon HMAC keys nor proxies arbitrary Dashboard routes.
- [Dashboard Control Panel](/botmux/en/dashboard.md): The botmux dashboard command prints the current rotating login-token URL for unified control across all daemons / bots in the browser. This is a rotating login token: a URL stays valid until botmux dashboard rotate replaces it and invalidates the old URL; the token is persisted and survives a botmux restart. The bare/current command reuses that token, creating the first one when absent. A successful ?t= visit just writes the same token into a cookie — it does not consume or revoke it, so the same URL logs in repeatedly until rotation. Sharing the URL ≈ sharing the login state, so keep it safe. Default port 7891, overridable via BOTMUX_DASHBOARD_PORT.
- [Decision Board and Steward](/botmux/en/decision-board.md): Make one bot your steward: it pushes forward the development tasks you hand it, and writes anything that needs your call onto the decision board. You write a decision per item (and paste screenshots), then click Submit once — the whole batch reaches the steward's session as one message, and the steward executes it item by item and writes the results back. Off by default. Deployments without a steward get no extra files, pages or prompt text.
- [Feishu Doc Comment Watching (/watch-comment)](/botmux/en/doc-comment.md): Turn a Feishu/Lark cloud doc into a session's input/output channel: after subscribing a doc, its comments feed into the session as messages, and the bot's replies are posted back into that comment's thread. Without leaving the doc you're working in, @the bot in a comment to ask a question or request a change — the reply shows up right in the comment thread. Great for "drive the AI while reading the doc" and in-place collaboration.
- [Environment Variables and File Locations](/botmux/en/env.md): Most configuration goes through bots.json / the dashboard — you usually don't need env vars. Only a few machine-level switches (bind address / port / backend type / external host) live in ~/.botmux/.env. This page also lists botmux's key file locations for backup / troubleshooting. Applies to: the dashboard / web terminal won't open or you need to change the bind address, pin a port, switch the pty/tmux backend, or find where config / logs / credentials live. This page covers botmux's own process environment. Which variables a session (CLI) receives is viewed and edited in the Dashboard under "Settings → Session environment" and "Bot settings → Advanced → Startup environment → Session environment"; see Session environment.
- [FAQ / Troubleshooting](/botmux/en/faq.md): Compiled from the README and high-frequency questions in the community group, and continuously expanded. For more pitfalls, see Common Pitfalls.
- [Create a Session Group in One Step](/botmux/en/group.md): /group <group name> (alias /g): automatically creates a new Lark group, invites you in, and transfers ownership to you, with the entire group serving as a single, independent CLI session (chat-scope). Great for spinning up a clean collaboration space dedicated to one project / task. The bot replies with a card: "✅ Created group 'card race-condition bug' 👉 <join link>". Click in and start chatting right away — the whole group is one independent session. When the group name is empty, a timestamp placeholder is used until the first message names the group (see below). After creation, no session is started automatically; enter the group and message the bot to start chatting.
- [Lifecycle Hooks](/botmux/en/hooks.md): botmux can invoke external commands when key lifecycle events occur. By default they are asynchronous: if a command fails, times out, or doesn't exist, it only writes to the log and never blocks botmux's main flow. There are also synchronous gates (mode: "sync"): prompt.submit decides whether a message reaches the CLI, while chat.bot_added decides whether enabled join auto-start may continue. See Synchronous gates.
- [Mention Policy (`mention-mode`)](/botmux/en/mention-mode.md): In a regular group, by default the bot responds only to messages that explicitly @-mention it. The mention policy controls when @ is not required; it is a routing rule for human messages in regular groups and has nothing to do with authorization — skipping @ never skips the talk gate, so someone without talk access is still blocked (see Permissions & Authorization).
- [Multi-bot Collaboration](/botmux/en/multi-bot.md): Multiple Lark bots can run on the same machine, and each bot can be bound to a different CLI. Add them to the same group and you can have different models "duke it out" against each other. <video src="https://magic-builder.tos-cn-beijing.volces.com/uploads/1780421535360_multibot-video.aud.mp4" controls preload="metadata" style={{width:'100%',borderRadius:'8px'}}></video>
- [Multi-Topic Orchestration Mode](/botmux/en/multi-topic.md): An upgrade to multi-bot collaboration: hand a big task to a main bot, and it automatically breaks the task into multiple sub-projects, opens several topics in the group, assigns a group of bots to each topic to work in parallel (commonly "one writes, one reviews"), uses a single Lark task checklist as a shared progress board, and finally collects the results and summarizes them for you. An ordinary group turns into a parallel workbench.
- [On-Call Mode](/botmux/en/oncall.md): Add a bot to an on-call / duty / alert group and bind it to a project directory. Then any member of the group can @ the bot to ask questions — no need to pick a repository, no need to start a new session — going straight into that project directory to chat. Especially suited to "many people, asking anytime, all asking about the same project" scenarios like duty groups, alert groups, and cross-team Q&A. Adding the bot to a group is not authorization by itself: being added writes no allowlist entry. Anyone-in-the-group Q&A takes effect only once the on-call binding is in place (or after a bare /grant opens the whole group); on an unbound, restricted bot, a non-listed member @-mentioning it is blocked and triggers a grant request card instead. See Permissions & Access · Being added to a group is not authorization.
- [Permissions & Authorization](/botmux/en/permissions.md): botmux permissions answer two questions: who can talk to the bot (canTalk) and who can change session state (canOperate — /cd, /restart, /close, card buttons). There are several authorization layers, from "a few named admins" to "the whole group can ask freely". This page covers all of them in one place.
- [Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them](/botmux/en/pitfalls.md): High-frequency, battle-tested pitfalls from the community group, sorted by how often they occur and their impact. When something misbehaves after install / upgrade, scan here first — most are known pitfalls, not new problems; for pure triage steps see General troubleshooting approach at the end.
- [Plugin Development and Market Registration](/botmux/en/plugins.md): A Botmux Plugin uses one publishable npm package to deliver Skills, MCP, CLI commands, a Dashboard page, and a Host Service. This guide is for plugin authors and operators. It covers the complete path from project creation and package validation to npm publishing and Plugin Market registration. Current boundary: the Plugin Market is a separate discovery index. Publishing a package to npm does not register it in the market, and the current stable Botmux release does not read that index during installation. The full npm package name is always the most reliable installation entry point.
- [Prerequisites](/botmux/en/prerequisites.md): Before installing botmux, make sure these are in place — many "installed but won't connect / sessions won't start" issues trace back to a missing prerequisite here (CLI not logged in, tmux missing, not on PATH). Applies to: any machine that will run the botmux daemon (dev machine / devbox / server). Doesn't apply: if you only @ a bot in a group someone else already set up — you don't need to install anything locally.
- [5-minute quick setup](/botmux/en/quickstart.md): 💡 TL;DR: curl -fsSL .../install.sh | sh → botmux setup (a single Lark QR scan creates the app + configures all permissions + publishes) → botmux start → botmux autostart enable → add the bot to a group and start chatting. Before you start: confirm the Prerequisites (target CLI installed and logged in, tmux) — a missing prerequisite here is the most common cause of "installed but won't connect."
- [Session Relay](/botmux/en/relay.md): Relay a running AI session from one group to another to continue there — the Lark message history stays in the source group, but the AI's memory / context carries over, so you can switch groups and keep chatting seamlessly. The command is /relay. A half-finished session can move house entirely, without losing any context: get a plan working in a private chat, then move it into the team group with one command so everyone can continue from that same context. What moves over is the same CLI process and the same memory — not a copy spun up fresh. Difference from Adopt: Adopt brings a process from your local tmux into Lark; Relay moves a session that's already running inside botmux from group A to group B.
- [Roles and Teams](/botmux/en/roles.md): Give each bot an independent persona per group, and form a "team roster" during multi-bot collaboration. The command is /role. This page covers two related but distinct capabilities: /role personas (one persona per bot, overridable per group — see below) and Role Switch (one bot owning multiple full roles, each with independent memory, switched by natural language per topic — an advanced feature).
- [File & Network Sandbox](/botmux/en/sandbox.md): Botmux provides multi-layered runtime isolation to safeguard your host development machine from accidental file modification and sensitive credential leakage. The file sandbox is one switch with three positions, configured per bot, fully supporting both Linux and macOS: Leaving sandbox out of bots.json (or setting false) means off; true is the same as "oncall". The legacy field readIsolation: true is now treated as allowlist isolation and is migrated automatically at daemon startup. 💡 Which mode should you choose?Exposing your bot to semi-trusted group members → choose allowlist isolation. SSH keys, tokens, credentials, and other projects are invisible by default, preventing reconnaissance and data leakage.Using the bot yourself for complex builds, scripts, or risky commands → choose scratch. No allowlist configuration needed; all dependencies and global tools just work, while any modification can be discarded cleanly without touching your real host disk. Scratch can read most files on the host, so it is not suitable for untrusted users.
- [Scheduled Tasks](/botmux/en/schedule.md): Supports three schedule types plus natural-language input. Tasks run at their configured execution position when due. In group chats, the default is chat top level, even when the task is created inside a topic. To continue in the current topic, explicitly pass --topic when creating the task through the CLI, or select the original topic under Execution position in the Dashboard. There are four execution positions: chat top level (the default; all top-level tasks in one group share the chat-scope session context), a specified topic (--topic, bound to one existing topic), a new topic per run (--new-topic, every run stands alone), and a dedicated task topic (opt-in; each task owns its own topic session — see below).
- [Session & Topic Model](/botmux/en/session-model.md): The key to understanding botmux is figuring out "which session a given message lands in" — confusions like "why does every @ feel like a fresh start that lost my context" and "how does a new group pull in history" all trace back to this. Applies to: when you're unsure which session a message went to, want to control new-vs-reused sessions, or are configuring in-group permissions.
- [Skill + CLI Interaction](/botmux/en/skill-cli.md): When a CLI enters a botmux session, it automatically gets ~/.botmux/bin in its PATH, along with a set of ready-to-use capabilities. This is the channel through which a CLI agent can proactively interact with a Lark topic — and "terminal has output but nothing was sent to Lark" usually traces back to the model not using this channel (see FAQ · C).
- [Slash Commands](/botmux/en/slash-commands.md): Just send these commands directly in a topic, and the daemon intercepts and handles them. Only the allowlisted commands in the passthrough section are forwarded verbatim to the underlying CLI; any other /xxx the daemon doesn't recognize is treated as ordinary conversation text and relayed as a normal message. Send /help anytime to view the full list.
- [Tmux Session Persistence](/botmux/en/tmux.md): tmux is botmux's default backend (PTY is retired and no longer an automatic fallback). Once tmux is installed, the CLI process stays persistent inside a tmux session, so restarting the daemon does not interrupt the CLI — which is the answer to the common worry "will a restart lose my context?": it won't.
- [Delivery when the original topic is unavailable](/botmux/en/topic-unavailable-policy.md): topicUnavailablePolicy is a per-bot setting. Configure it under Dashboard → Reply Delivery, or with /botconfig set topicUnavailablePolicy stop. The setting applies immediately to subsequent CLI sends and automatic final replies. Unthreaded broadcasts have no source topic to check. An already-delivered send that the turn ledger replays performs no new publication. TOPIC_SEND_BLOCKED means the queried message is withdrawn. TOPIC_SEND_CHECK_FAILED means the query failed or did not prove the message is available; retry the query on the same route. Neither outcome grants permission to publish elsewhere. A provider-side withdrawal after a successful lookup also prevents the existing quote-to-chat fallback in stop mode. Set the value back to legacy, or unset it with /botconfig unset topicUnavailablePolicy, to restore default behavior. This option does not cancel an executing task or prove that its original content should be deleted. Each send caches successful lookups for at most one second within that delivery. CLI preparation and the first provider-effect fence each perform a fresh lookup; repeated checks at the same fence reuse that result. Failed or unknown checks are never cached, and the provider withdrawal response still blocks quote fallback. CLI refusals use exit code 2 and botmux send refused: …. Permanent withdrawal (including provider code 230011) stops automatic-final retries immediately and marks the session as blocked in Dashboard's needs-you column. The final output remains undelivered; no notice is published to a different conversation.
- [Turn Results](/botmux/en/turn-results.md): TurnResult separates native execution, final output, and acknowledged delivery. Reading a result does not run a model, send a message, or authorize a business action.
- [Voice Summary](/botmux/en/voice.md): Turn the AI's text reply into a voice message in your Lark group with one click. Every reply card gets a "🔊 Voice Summary" button at the bottom — tap it, and the bot condenses that reply into spoken language, synthesizes a voice bubble, and sends it to the current topic. <video src="https://magic-builder.tos-cn-beijing.volces.com/uploads/1780421547656_voice-video.aud.mp4" controls preload="metadata" style={{width:'100%',borderRadius:'8px'}}></video> On-demand trigger: Nothing is generated automatically by default — it only happens when you tap, so you don't get a long voice clip attached to every reply.Condense first, then synthesize: After you tap, the model compresses the original reply into a few spoken sentences (stripping out code, paths, links, and other content that doesn't read aloud well), so what you hear is a "plain-speech" summary rather than the original text read verbatim.Permission gate: Only members with "chat / operate" permission on that bot can tap it; others who tap get a "needs authorization" prompt.Generated only once per reply: The voice for a given reply is generated only once, so multiple taps won't flood the chat. Voice is an optional advanced feature: you must first configure a text-to-speech (TTS) engine; until you do, the button won't appear on reply cards.
- [Web Terminal (interactive)](/botmux/en/web-terminal.md): Every session except a ZMX-backed one comes with an xterm.js-based Web Terminal, at an address like http://<WEB_EXTERNAL_HOST>:<port>; for ZMX, use botmux list or zmx attach to enter a local terminal and see the ZMX backend guide.
- [Connectors (Webhook)](/botmux/en/webhook.md): Let external systems (monitoring alerts, CI, tickets, scheduled scripts…) trigger a bot to speak in a group or run a workflow via a webhook. The gateway doesn't parse each platform's format — it hands the raw event as-is to the model to read for itself, so a new system needs almost zero adaptation. Create and manage these on the "Connectors" page of the Dashboard Control Panel. Currently in beta.
- [Local Whiteboard](/botmux/en/whiteboard.md): Multiple bots / sessions in the same Lark group share a local markdown whiteboard that captures the "current project state" (goals / how work is organized / core plan / key progress / next steps) across sessions and bots. The board is a latest-state snapshot: update overwrites the whole thing instead of appending history, so a later agent reads the current consensus directly instead of scrolling chat history. It fits multi-agent collaboration, long-task checkpoints, and cross-topic handoff. Disabled by default. It's an optional enhancement — when off, no board is created, no session is bound, no prompt is injected, and an agent's read/write commands are rejected.
- [Workflow (Experimental)](/botmux/en/workflow.md): One fuzzy goal → auto-interrogate, orchestrate a DAG, execute concurrently; a flow that works can be saved as a Saved Workflow and reused. Runs are stored in ~/.botmux/v3-runs; their state lives in the Dashboard's v3 view (every Feishu card carries a "Web details" link straight to it). ⚠️ Workflow is off by default. Turn on the "Workflow" switch on the Dashboard settings page, or set BOTMUX_WORKFLOW_ENABLED=true. While it is off, ad-hoc orchestration and running/saving Saved Workflows are refused, but in-flight runs can still be managed with botmux workflow cancel / retry / grant.
- [ZMX Session Backend](/botmux/en/zmx.md): ZMX is an optional persistent-session backend for botmux. It is intended for macOS and Linux hosts that want a lightweight session daemon to keep the CLI alive, with a native local attach available whenever the complete terminal experience is needed. ZMX is an explicit opt-in backend. botmux does not install ZMX, and merely finding it on PATH never makes botmux select it automatically.
